passages.title: Fiddy Working Heritage Farm
content: 📌 Fiddy Working Heritage Farm
Advice for farm visitors
Visitors should:

• avoid causing harm to any [ _____ ]
• never touch any [ _____ ]
• have [ _____ ] on their feet
• leave [ _____ ] outside the farm, apart from specified exceptions
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to Fiddy Working Heritage Farm and explaining its layout. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 20. Welcome to Fiddy Working Heritage Farm.

[00:55] AUDIO: This open-air museum shows visitors what farming and country life in England were like towards the end of the 19th century. The farm represents that period and all the staff, including me, wear clothes from the time. Before we continue, I need to give you a few safety reminders. This is a genuine working farm, so please take care not to scare or hurt any of the animals.

[01:23] AUDIO: We keep many here, including several breeds that have now become quite uncommon. Please keep well away from the tools too. Some have very sharp ends and could cause an injury, so don't touch them. The ground is uneven in places and sandals can make it easy to slip.

[01:46] AUDIO: I'm pleased that everyone today is wearing shoes, which is what we always recommend. Children of every age are welcome. Even the youngest visitors normally enjoy seeing the ducks and lambs, so feel free to bring children on a future visit. I don't believe anyone has brought a dog today.

[02:09] AUDIO: If you have, it must remain in the car park unless it is a guide dog. As you can imagine, dogs could create serious difficulties on a farm. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[03:07] AUDIO: Let me now explain how the farm is arranged. The building where you purchased your tickets is the new barn, directly on your right. We're standing at the start of the main path leading towards the farmland with the car park on the left. In the corner of the car park, beside the main path, you'll see the scarecrow.

[03:30] AUDIO: Traditionally, scarecrows keep birds away from crops, although ours is a permanent sculpture. It's taller than a person and visible from some distance. Straight ahead is the maze. It stands opposite the new barn, next to the smaller path that branches to the right.

[03:49] AUDIO: Its hedges are too high for small children to see over, but the maze itself is compact, so nobody should get lost. Further along the main path, there's a bridge over the fish pool. To reach the café, walk towards the bridge and turn right immediately before it. Follow that side path, the café is on the first bend.

[04:14] AUDIO: The building used to be the schoolhouse and is more than a century old. We also offer workshops in traditional skills, including woodwork and basket making. Examples of what participants produce, as well as information about the courses, are available in the black barn. Take the side path on the right beside the new barn.

[04:40] AUDIO: The black barn is where that path makes its first turn. I should mention the picnic facilities, since some of you have lunch with you. You're welcome to eat in the field, but please clear everything away afterwards. If you would rather sit under cover, cross the bridge.

[05:01] AUDIO: The covered picnic area is on the right, close to the farmyard. Finally, there's Fiddy House. From this point, go over the bridge and take the footpath across the field to the left of the farmyard. It leads to the house and gives an excellent view for photographs.

[05:21] AUDIO: The house is privately occupied though, so visitors cannot enter. If everyone is ready, we'll begin our tour. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Study On Gender In Physics
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Study On Gender In Physics"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:02] NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing research into gender and achievement in physics. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 27. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 27.
[00:53] LISA: Greg, I finally read the article you recommended about gender and physics.
[00:58] GREG: The one on Akira Miyaki's study of university students. Oh, yeah. I found it unusual that the research team included both psychologists and physicists.
[01:11] LISA: So did I. At first, I wasn't sure which students took part. They weren't physics majors. They were studying subjects grouped under STEM, science, technology, engineering and…
[01:26] GREG: Mathematics? Exactly. But physics formed part of all their degree courses.

[01:31] LISA: Right. As I understand it, Miyaki's group began with the fact that women are less well represented in introductory college physics classes. On average, the women who enroll also achieve lower results than the men, although the reason isn't clear.
[01:51] GREG: Yes, the researchers were essentially looking for a way to raise the women's performance. To do that, they first had to understand the problem better.
[02:02] LISA: Let me see if I remember… The women in the physics class believed the male students thought women were poor at the subject and expected them to get low test scores.

[02:14] GREG: That was the women's belief, and it made them anxious, which did affect their results. But the belief itself was mistaken. The men weren't making those assumptions about the female students.
[02:28] LISA: Miyaki's team then used a very simple activity. The students completed some writing before attending physics class. What was it called?

[02:39] GREG: Values affirmation. They wrote an essay about things with personal significance. It wasn't specifically about physics, but about broader matters such as music or people who were important in their lives.
[02:54] LISA: So the exercise was intended to put them in a more positive frame of mind.

[03:00] GREG: Yes. Expressing those thoughts in words could help them relax and overcome psychological barriers to good performance. What surprised the researchers was the scale of the effect. This single activity moved the women's physics grades from the C range into the B range.
[03:19] LISA: That's a substantial improvement. Not quite an A, but impressive. It also suggests the women had previously been performing well below their real ability compared with the men.

[03:33] GREG: True. Still, the article omitted several details. For example, did the students write only once or on several occasions? More importantly, were they told why they were doing the exercise?
[03:48] GREG: That information could have influenced the outcome.
[03:51] LISA: Because if they knew the researchers expected it to improve their performance, they might try to produce the predicted result.
[03:59] GREG: Exactly.
[04:03] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30.
[04:46] GREG: For our own project then, I thought we could conduct a similar investigation and test whether the writing activity itself really produced the improvement.
[04:56] LISA: We could ask one group to write about a completely different factual subject, perhaps a general knowledge topic.
[05:05] GREG: Perhaps. Or one half could complete a writing task while the other half did something different, such as speaking.

[05:14] LISA: Another possibility is for half to do the same personal writing as in the original study and half to complete a factual writing task. That would show whether the topic was responsible rather than some other feature.

[05:30] GREG: Good. At our meeting with the supervisor on Monday, we can say we've chosen the project. We should prepare our aims. We also need to find the original study since the article was only a summary.
[05:44] LISA: I read another paper by Smolinski. It compared how women and men performed in mixed teams, single-sex teams and individually during class activities.
[05:57] GREG: Let me guess, the women did better in groups.

[06:00] LISA: That's what I expected too. In fact, teamwork made no difference. Men and women achieved the same results whether they worked in teams or alone. It probably isn't especially relevant to our study.
[06:15] GREG: My concern is whether we can complete everything in the time available.
[06:20] LISA: We should manage now that the project is clearer. I'm still uncertain how we'll measure whether the participants make progress.
[06:28] GREG: We may need guidance on that. We also have to choose an appropriate sample size. Not too large or too small.
[06:39] LISA: That should be manageable. What should we do next? We could check the science class timetable, but making an appointment with one of the science professors would be more useful.
[06:52] GREG: Good idea. We might even observe a class.
[06:54] LISA: What would that add?
[06:56] GREG: Fair point. Let's follow your suggestion.
[07:02] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

transcript: [00:02] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about biodiversity in the world's oceans. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. I've been studying ocean biodiversity, meaning the range of species found in the world's seas.

[00:55] AUDIO: Around 20 years ago, biologists introduced the concept of biodiversity hotspots. These are places with an exceptionally varied collection of species. Madagascar is one terrestrial example. Hotspots matter because they help scientists identify the key locations where conservation work should be concentrated.

[01:19] AUDIO: Such areas are fairly easy to recognise on land. Until recently, however, scientists knew very little about the distribution and variety of ocean life, and did not even know whether marine hotspots existed. In 2005, the Canadian biologist Boris Warm analysed information on ocean species supplied by the fishing industry. He identified five hotspots for large marine predators, such as sharks, and examined their shared features.

[01:53] AUDIO: He expected all of them to contain unusually large quantities of food. That was true of four, but the fifth had relatively little food available. One condition common to every site was comparatively warm water at the ocean surface, even when deeper water was cool. This appeared to help support a wide variety of large predators.

[02:21] AUDIO: Warmth alone was insufficient, though. The water also had to contain enough oxygen to meet the high metabolic needs of those fish. Two years later, in 2007, Lisa Balance, a researcher based in California, also searched for ocean hotspots. Her focus wasn't fish, but marine mammals, including seals.

[02:46] AUDIO: She found three hotspot locations, all situated where different ocean currents meet. Such boundaries appear to contain plentiful plankton, on which some of the mammals feed. Protecting endangered species requires as much reliable information as possible. An international initiative called the Census of Marine Life has surveyed oceans worldwide, including the Arctic.

[03:18] AUDIO: Researchers there made the surprising discovery that many species live beneath the ice, sometimes below a layer up to 20 metres thick. Some had never previously been recorded, and octopus species were among those found. Other teams in the same project studied completely different habitats on the seafloor. They discovered large numbers of organisms, living around volcanoes, drawn by the heat and nutrients.

[03:53] AUDIO: Even so, biologists still cannot judge precisely how serious the danger is for every individual species. The Global Marine Species Assessment is compiling a list of threatened species. Its researchers consider population size, the number of members of a species in a particular place, and geographical distribution, which is especially difficult for highly mobile fish. Their third measure is the rate at which a species is declining.

[04:26] AUDIO: Only 1,500 species have been assessed so far, but the target is 20,000. For each species, the collected data are used to create a map of its distribution. Eventually, these maps should reveal both where most species occur and where they face the greatest threats. What, then, can we do to maintain biodiversity in the oceans?

[04:58] AUDIO: First, more marine reserves are needed so that species have protected areas. Some already exist, but there are too few. We should also establish migration corridors. Leatherback turtles, for example, live on the high seas but nest along the American coast, so they need safe routes between those places.

[05:20] AUDIO: Fishing quotas should also be reduced to limit the overfishing of endangered species. Finally, there is the problem of bycatch. Unwanted fish taken by commercial boats and returned to the sea, often already dead or dying. More selective equipment would allow crews to catch only fish intended for consumption and would greatly reduce this problem.
[05:49] AUDIO: Now, are there any questions? That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript: [00:01] NARRATOR: You will hear a young man phoning to ask about joining a youth council. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
[00:50] CAROLINE: Good morning, youth council. Caroline speaking.
[00:54] ROGER: Hello, I'm interested in standing for election to the youth council and I was advised to call you.
[01:00] CAROLINE: That's excellent. Could I take your name?
[01:04] ROGER: Yes, it's Roger Brown.
[01:06] CAROLINE: Thank you. I'm Caroline, the council administrator. Do you already know much about the youth council, Roger?
[01:14] ROGER: I've spoken to Stephanie. I believe she's the council chair.
[01:19] CAROLINE: That's right.
[01:20] ROGER: She explained quite a lot. Young people can discuss local matters and make proposals to the town council, for instance. That's what attracted me.
[01:31] CAROLINE: Good. I'll record a few details. How old are you? The council is for people between 13 and 18.
[01:39] ROGER: I've just turned 18.
[01:41] CAROLINE: Where are you living at present?
[01:44] ROGER: It's slightly complicated. I'm trying to find a flat here, so during the week, from Monday to Friday, I'm staying in a hostel. At weekends, I return to my parents' home.
[01:57] CAROLINE: Which address should we use to send information about the council?
[02:02] ROGER: My parents' address, please. 17 Buckley Street, Stamford, Lincolnshire. Buckley is B-U-C-K-L-E-I-G-H.
[02:19] CAROLINE: I know Stamford. It's a lovely place. What's the postcode?
[02:30] CAROLINE: Thanks. Are you employed here or are you studying?
[02:34] ROGER: I began university a couple of weeks ago, and I also work a few hours each week in a part-time job.
[02:41] CAROLINE: What kind of work is it?
[02:43] ROGER: I've had several jobs. I recently finished a temporary contract as a courier, and now I'm a waiter in one of the larger hotels.
[02:54] CAROLINE: That must leave very little study time.
[02:57] ROGER: It isn't too difficult. I can fit everything in.
[03:00] CAROLINE: What subjects are you taking?
[03:03] ROGER: Eventually, I'd like to enter Parliament, so Politics is my major. That's also one reason the Youth Council seems important to me.
[03:13] CAROLINE: You have a minor subject too, don't you? Many students choose Economics.
[03:19] ROGER: Mine is History, although honestly, it hasn't been as interesting as I'd hoped.
[03:29] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[04:14] CAROLINE: With university and your job, do you still have time for hobbies?
[04:18] ROGER: I spend a great deal of time cycling, both around town to reach university and work, and on longer journeys, such as riding from here to London.
[04:30] CAROLINE: That's impressive. Anything else?
[04:34] ROGER: To relax, I'm keen on the cinema. I used to go at least weekly, though I can't manage that so often now.
[04:42] CAROLINE: Are you certain you'll have enough time for council duties?
[04:47] ROGER: Yes. I've worked out that I can cut my working hours and free up the time.
[04:52] CAROLINE: Is there a particular area of the council's work that interests you?
[04:58] ROGER: My sister is blind, so I'd especially like to support disabled young people and help improve their quality of life.
[05:06] CAROLINE: That's very worthwhile. The usual way to become involved is to be nominated by people you know.
[05:13] ROGER: How should I arrange that?
[05:16] CAROLINE: Speak to Geoffrey, our elections officer. I can set up a meeting with him here at the council office.
[05:24] ROGER: Yes, please.
[05:26] CAROLINE: He'll be here next Monday, if that works for you.
[05:29] ROGER: That's the 14th, isn't it?
[05:31] CAROLINE: Yes.
[05:32] ROGER: Late afternoon would suit me.
[05:34] CAROLINE: What time would you suggest? He normally leaves at about half past five.
[05:40] ROGER: Would 4.30 be possible? My final class ends at four, which gives me enough time to reach the office.
[05:48] CAROLINE: That's fine. Could you also give me a contact phone number?
[05:52] ROGER: Certainly. My mobile is 07788 136711.
[06:03] CAROLINE: Thank you. We'll look forward to meeting you next week.
[06:07] ROGER: Thanks very much. Goodbye.
[06:09] CAROLINE: Goodbye.
[06:12] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a member of staff introducing two new employees to a theatre. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Hello, it's great to meet you both.

[00:51] AUDIO: I'm Jodie, and I'll be responsible for helping you during your first month at the Amersham Theatre. I'll begin by explaining a little about the theatre, and afterwards I'll introduce you to two other members of staff. The building is old and has been updated several times. As you can see, a major refurbishment is underway now.

[01:15] AUDIO: The inside has just been repainted, while work on the exterior is due to begin soon and will be considerable. Because the project has exceeded its budget, the planned elevator has been delayed, so I hope you don't mind using the stairs. When the theatre was constructed, audiences were generally smaller, and the seats were packed closely together. We've installed larger seats with more legroom.

[01:46] AUDIO: There are fewer of them, but they can be moved easily to create different performance spaces. Several former storerooms have also been converted for other uses, including meetings. We make a real effort to involve the public. One method is to offer backstage tours, which allow visitors to explore the building and discover how a theatre functions.

[02:13] AUDIO: They've become very popular. Visitors often ask for lunch or coffee, so a café may be opened later. At present, we have a bookshop specialising in drama, and it attracts plenty of customers. Two large rooms will be redecorated next month, and then offered for conferences and private events.

[02:37] AUDIO: We're also thinking about renting costumes to amateur theatre groups. We recently introduced a workshop programme, Open to Everyone. We eventually hope to provide acting courses, but suitable instructors have been harder to find than expected. There is strong interest in the technical aspects of production, and the lighting workshop is already running, very successfully.

[03:06] AUDIO: A sound course will begin next month. Make-up workshops are being considered for the future. Unexpectedly, puppet-making has been extremely successful. One of our employees makes puppets as a hobby and volunteered to teach it.

[03:23] AUDIO: Demand was so high that the workshop now runs monthly. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Let me now describe the building's layout.

[04:19] AUDIO: The auditoriums, stage and actors' dressing rooms are all below ground. Most of the rooms here on the ground floor aren't normally seen by the public, because many are internal rooms, they receive light through roof windows. We're standing in the foyer, and you may be wondering why the box office isn't here in the place audiences would expect. You may have noticed it as you entered.

[04:47] AUDIO: It forms part of the same building but is next door, with its own entrance from the street. To find the theatre manager's office, cross the foyer, pass through the double doors and turn right. Follow the corridor to the end. The office door is on the left.

[05:08] AUDIO: The computerised stage lights are operated from the lighting box at the rear of the building. Go through the double doors and turn left, then turn right by the water cooler. At the end, turn right once more. The lighting box is the second room along that corridor.

[05:28] AUDIO: It has a window looking into the auditorium below. The artistic director's office is also through the double doors. Turn right, and it is the first room on the right. The last place for now is the relaxation room, where we're going next.
[05:49] AUDIO: Please follow me. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Rocky Bay Field Trip
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Rocky Bay Field Trip"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two biology students discussing a report on their field trip to Rocky Bay. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:50] HELEN: Hi Colin, I've brought my notes from our biology field trip to Rocky Bay, so we can start writing the report on the research we carried out together.
[00:59] COLIN: Good, I've got mine as well. Let's begin with the aims.
[01:04] HELEN: Alright, what did you write?

[01:07] COLIN: I mentioned gaining experience of the various procedures used during fieldwork. We should also include an aim about the factors that make different organisms select particular habitats.
[01:20] HELEN: Agreed. Should we say something about learning how to protect species at risk of extinction?
[01:27] COLIN: In the aims? We didn't actually investigate that.
[01:31] HELEN: True. Now, what about the equipment list? Why were we told to bring a ruler?
[01:38] COLIN: It was meant for measuring the slope of the shore. We didn't use it because our task was measuring wind direction, and we had remembered the compass for that.
[01:48] HELEN: But we forgot the string we needed to hold up in the wind. Mr Blake certainly complained about that.
[01:56] COLIN: He did. Fortunately, another student lent us some.
[02:01] HELEN: The next part is the procedure. I sent you my draft.
[02:04] COLIN: Yes, it was clear, but there's too much detail about our departure and return times, and the way we shared the research tasks.
[02:13] HELEN: I'll shorten that section.
[02:15] COLIN: Then we need a detailed account of our investigation methods, starting with wave speed. I hadn't expected it to be so easy to carry out.

[02:25] HELEN: Neither had I. I imagined some advanced equipment, but we simply stood there and counted the waves each minute. It wasn't especially accurate, though it was adequate. The method for measuring salt levels was more interesting.
[02:42] COLIN: In the rock pool water?
[02:44] HELEN: Yes. I wanted to confirm the chemicals used when we analysed the samples in the lab. Were they potassium chromate and silver nitrate?
[02:55] COLIN: That's correct.

[02:57] HELEN: We also need the map of the shoreline, which you left entirely to me. It had to be drawn at low tide, and that part was fine. The problem was that I began down on the beach, then realised I needed to stand higher up for a clearer view. So I had to start again.
[03:17] HELEN: Luckily, I had squared paper, or keeping the scale correct would have been difficult.
[03:23] COLIN: The finished map looks good. We could compare it with an online map of the area, and see whether anything needs changing.
[03:32] HELEN: I searched, but couldn't find one. You took photographs, though, didn't you?
[03:38] COLIN: Yes, I can email them to you.
[03:40] HELEN: Great. I'll check the map against those photographs, make any corrections, and then scan it into the report.
[03:51] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:35] HELEN: For the findings section, I thought we could organise the results by the different shore zones and the difficulties organisms face in each. Starting with the highest area.
[04:47] COLIN: The splash zone?
[04:49] HELEN: Yes, we mainly found small shellfish with hard, strong shells for protection.
[04:55] COLIN: Protection from predators that might eat them?
[04:58] HELEN: That isn't their principal threat. The shells stop them losing water because they're exposed to the air for most of the time.

[05:06] COLIN: And since they're exposed, they also need shelter or some form of cover to prevent them becoming too hot. In the middle and lower zones, closer to the sea, we should discuss wave action.
[05:20] HELEN: Yes, including the structures organisms develop so they aren't washed away or smashed against the rocks.
[05:28] COLIN: I haven't written anything about geological change. I'm not sure what to include.
[05:34] HELEN: It wasn't our main focus. Perhaps we should find some websites.
[05:38] COLIN: Good idea. I have Mr Blake's geology lecture notes, but they're too broad. We could ask him which titles on the reading list would help most.

[05:51] HELEN: Now, I've drafted the section on possible sources of error. I considered sample size and whether it was large enough for general conclusions, but our sample was actually quite substantial.
[06:03] COLIN: It was, and the general observation method seemed dependable. The precise counts may be less reliable, however.
[06:12] HELEN: We could have failed to count some organisms if they were hidden beneath rocks. I also wondered whether our habitat descriptions were accurate, but I think those were acceptable.
[06:24] COLIN: I agree. Our descriptions of the smaller organisms lack detail, but we're sufficient here. I'm less confident that every species was identified correctly.
[06:37] HELEN: Then we'll include both of those limitations. Now, what about?
[06:44] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: The Taylor Concert Hall
content: 📌 The Taylor Concert Hall

Introduction
An architect designing a public building may have to consider its
purpose physical and [ _____ ] contextsymbolic significance
Location and concept of the concert hall
constructed on the site of an abandoned [ _____ ]situated next to a [ _____ ]design concept centred on a mystery
Building design
pedestrians approach across a [ _____ ]the whole building resembles a [ _____ ]one outside wall functions as a huge [ _____ ]
Inside the auditorium
the floor rests on enormous [ _____ ] padsthe locally sourced wooden walls are [ _____ ]ceiling panels and wall [ _____ ] can alter the acoustics

Evaluation
Some critics consider the building's [ _____ ] style unsuitable.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about the architectural design of the Taylor Concert Hall. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. We've been considering the issues architects face when designing homes.

[00:54] AUDIO: I'll now turn to public buildings using the recently completed Taylor Concert Hall in this city as an example. As with a home, the architect of a public building must first consider its function. For example, is its main purpose entertainment, education, or administration? A second consideration is context.

[01:16] AUDIO: This obviously includes the physical setting, but also the building's social significance and its relationship with the community it serves. Finally, when a major public building is planned, the architect may seek a central symbolic idea, a metaphor that informs both its design and use. Let's apply these principles to the Taylor Concert Hall. Its site lies in a neglected district that previous redevelopment schemes had overlooked.

[01:50] AUDIO: A disused factory had occupied the land for several years. The area is some distance from the high-rise offices of the business district and the main shopping center, although it is only a kilometer from the ring road. The site sits alongside a canal on its northern side. It was once used by boats delivering raw materials when manufacturing operated there.

[02:19] AUDIO: The chosen architect, Tom Harrison, felt that the greatest challenge was the absence of any significant neighboring buildings. The future importance of a concert hall in such a rundown location was still uncertain. To express that uncertainty, he based the design on the idea of a mystery, something whose meaning remains to be uncovered. How does the building convey this idea?

[02:49] AUDIO: Harrison created a pedestrian approach and incorporated the water beside the site. Visitors must cross a bridge to reach the entrance. As they see the hall first from far away and then close up, he wanted to build a sense of anticipation. The overall form was intended to resemble a box.

[03:10] AUDIO: The first surface visible to approaching visitors is the southern wall, a tall, flat wall without windows. Although that might appear unwelcoming, it creates curiosity about the interior. The wall also serves another function. At night, projectors turn it into a vast screen on which images are displayed.

[03:36] AUDIO: The auditorium seats 1,500 people. Its floor rests on ten enormous pads made from rubber, which absorb vibrations from outside and prevent them reaching the hall. The walls consist of several layers of honey-colored wood from local beech trees. To improve the auditorium's acoustics and amplify sound, the walls are curved rather than straight.

[04:04] AUDIO: The acoustic properties can also be adjusted for different orchestra sizes and styles of music. Nine motorized panels in the ceiling can be moved separately while curtains on the walls can be opened or closed to alter the sound. Public response to the new building has generally been favorable, although some architectural critics are less enthusiastic. Despite Harrison's use of local materials, they describe the building's style as international rather than local, and argue that it does not express the surrounding landscape or society.
[04:47] AUDIO: That is the end of Part Four. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part Four.

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking a tourist information advisor about free activities in the Burnham area. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:49] MARTIN: Good morning. Burnham tourist information. Martin speaking.

[00:53] SUE: Oh, hello. I noticed a poster advertising free activities locally, and it's said to call this number for details. I'm visiting Burnham with my husband and our two children for a few days, arriving on either 27th or 28th June. And I'd like ideas for the 29th.

[01:15] MARTIN: Certainly. Let's begin with two events intended especially for children. The art gallery is running an event called Family Welcome that day with activities and trails around the gallery.
[01:28] SUE: Wow, that sounds good. So when does it begin?

[01:33] MARTIN: The gallery itself opens at 10, but Family Welcome runs from 10.30 until 2. The gallery remains open until 5. Several times that day, they'll also screen a short film produced by the gallery. It shows how ceramics are made, and children will have equipment and materials to try the process themselves.
[01:54] MARTIN: At the previous event, the film focused on painting and was very popular, so this time they're preparing one about sculpture.
[02:02] SUE: Oh, I like that. What else is happening in Burnham?
[02:06] MARTIN: Well, does your family enjoy music?
[02:09] SUE: Very much.

[02:10] MARTIN: Then there are several free concerts at different times, one or two in the morning, most of them around lunchtime, and another couple in the evening. The music ranges from pop to Latin American.
[02:23] SUE: Latin American music might be fun. So when is that concert?

[02:29] MARTIN: It's performed several times at different venues. There's a performance in the Central Library at one. Let me see… There's another at four in the City Museum, and a longer concert in the theater at 7.30 that evening.
[02:43] SUE: Great. I'll mention that to my family.
[02:47] MARTIN: Well, you may also be interested in the boat race on the river.
[02:51] SUE: Yes, please tell me about it.
[02:53] MARTIN: It starts at Offord Marina, north of Burnham, and finishes at Summer Pool. Charlesworth Bridge offers the best view, although it becomes quite crowded.
[03:04] SUE: Who will be competing?

[03:07] MARTIN: Local boat clubs, and the standard is excellent. One club won the West of England Regional Championship in May this year, the first Burnham team ever to do so. As a result, it will represent the region at next year's National Championship.
[03:27] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:10] SUE: I've also heard about Paxton Nature Reserve. It's a good place to spot unusual birds, isn't it?

[04:17] MARTIN: Yes, throughout the year. The Reserve has both a lake and a river, which form an excellent habitat, so bring binoculars if you have some. At present, you can also see several unusual flowers because Paxton has a rare type of soil. They're looking particularly good now.
[04:39] SUE: Well, my husband will be very interested in those.
[04:43] MARTIN: There will also be a talk and slide presentation about mushrooms. Afterwards, visitors can collect some and examine the different varieties.
[04:53] SUE: Can children swim in the river?

[04:56] MARTIN: Yes. One section of the river has been fenced to make it safe for children. The water is very shallow and a lifeguard is present whenever it is open. The lake is too deep, so swimming there is prohibited.
[05:12] SUE: We'll bring there swimming things in case we visit Paxton. How long is the drive from Burnham?
[05:19] MARTIN: About 20 minutes. Parking is extremely limited though, so the bus is usually easier and takes roughly the same amount of time.
[05:29] SUE: I'll discuss all these possibilities with the family. Thank you very much.
[05:33] MARTIN: You're welcome.
[05:34] SUE: Goodbye.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Changes In Barford"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a town council representative speaking at a public meeting about changes in Barford. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. First, thank you all for attending this public meeting about our town's future.

[00:55] AUDIO: Our first speaker is Shona Ferguson from Barford Town Council. Thank you. I'll begin with a little background and then invite your comments on plan developments. As everyone here knows, Barford has altered considerably over the past 50 years.

[01:15] AUDIO: Let me summarise the main changes. Half a century ago buses connected nearly every part of Barford with nearby towns and villages, and most residents used them regularly. Today, however, operators concentrate only on routes carrying the largest numbers of passengers, leaving some districts without a service. Replacing the old, uncomfortable vehicles with modern buses has made little difference to passenger numbers.

[01:48] AUDIO: Some people blame expensive fares, but compared with average earnings, fares are not much higher than they were 50 years ago. The road network has also changed. The town centre was recently closed to cars on a trial basis, making it safer for pedestrians, though its overall effect is still being assessed. New cycle lanes separating bicycles from cars on most main roads have proved far more popular than predicted, reducing traffic and improving air quality.

[02:25] AUDIO: The council has not succeeded in securing a bypass, although we still hope the government will reconsider. Shopping patterns have changed too. Many residents remember a town centre packed with shoppers, but numbers have fallen for years, despite measures such as providing additional car parks. Some people combine shopping with a meal or a visit to a café.

[02:53] AUDIO: Most local shops are small, independent businesses, which has advantages. But many customers travel to larger nearby towns, for supermarkets and department stores, because Barford has so few major chain retailers. As for healthcare, several practices provide family doctors. There are fewer practices than there were 50 years ago, although each now serves many more patients.

[03:23] AUDIO: Barford's hospital closed 15 years ago, so residents must travel elsewhere for hospital treatment. On the positive side, the town has more dentists than before. Employment has changed as well. Growth in the number of schools and colleges means education now employs more people than any other sector.

[03:49] AUDIO: Service industries such as accountancy and website design have become more important, while manufacturing has not declined as sharply as it has elsewhere. content: Subject of drawingChange requiredA [ _____ ] surrounded by treesInclude Malcolm and a [ _____ ] that notices himPeople [ _____ ] outside the forestAdd Malcolm sitting on a tree trunk and [ _____ ]Ice-skaters on frozen [ _____ ]Give every person a [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Helen and Jeremy, discussing an art project. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:49] JEREMY: Hello, Helen. Sorry I'm late.
[00:52] HELEN: Hi, Jeremy. That's all right. We should probably review our progress on the project.
[00:57] JEREMY: Yes. I've examined the illustrations you made for my story, the forest, and they're excellent. They create exactly the atmosphere I imagined while writing it.
[01:11] HELEN: I'm pleased you like them.
[01:12] JEREMY: I only have a few changes to suggest.
[01:15] HELEN: Go ahead.
[01:16] JEREMY: First, the picture of the cave. The trees surrounding it are very effective, but the scene feels rather still. It needs some movement.
[01:27] HELEN: I agree. Nothing is happening. Perhaps I could include the boy, Malcolm, walking towards it.
[01:36] JEREMY: Yes. Add Malcolm. Could you also include a tiger, the one he becomes friendly with later? It might be under a tree cleaning itself.
[01:46] HELEN: Then the tiger could pause and notice Malcolm as he walks past.
[01:51] JEREMY: That would work well.
[01:52] HELEN: I'll try that.
[01:53] JEREMY: Next is the picture of the men and women dancing just outside the forest. There's already plenty happening in it.
[02:02] HELEN: You originally wanted them watching a carnival procession, but I thought that would make the image overcrowded. Does the current version work?
[02:13] JEREMY: Yes. I like it. I'd only ask you to add Malcolm without altering the rest.
[02:18] HELEN: He could sit on the tree trunk on the right.
[02:21] JEREMY: That's fine.
[02:22] HELEN: Should he be watching the others?
[02:26] JEREMY: No. He has been excluded from the enjoyment, so show him crying. That will contrast with the following illustration, where he laughs at the carnival clowns.
[02:38] HELEN: All right.
[02:39] JEREMY: Then there's the scene showing people ice skating in the forest.
[02:43] HELEN: I wasn't satisfied with it. They're meant to be skating on grass, aren't they?
[02:49] JEREMY: Yes. Grass that has frozen over. At present, it doesn't look convincing.
[02:56] HELEN: I understand. I'll redraw it.
[02:59] JEREMY: Their woolen hats are good. Perhaps each skater could have a scarf too.
[03:04] HELEN: That's straightforward. The scarves can trail behind them, making the skaters appear to be moving quickly.
[03:11] JEREMY: Great. That covers all the illustrations.
[03:15] HELEN: So your story is written and I only need to finish its pictures while my story and your illustrations are complete.
[03:26] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.

[04:09] HELEN: We now need to decide precisely what the accompanying report should contain and how to share the writing. Should we include a section explaining how we planned the overall project? That seems important.
[04:26] JEREMY: Yes. Since most of the planning ideas came from you, why don't you produce the first draft? Afterwards, we can review and discuss it together.
[04:35] HELEN: That sounds fair. I could also describe how we developed the ideas for our two stories.
[04:43] JEREMY: I've already begun writing about how I developed mine. You should do the same for yours, and we can include both accounts.
[04:52] HELEN: What about interpreting the stories? Should we explain what we believe they demonstrate, such as the importance of helping others?
[05:01] JEREMY: That will happen later. Everyone in the class will read the other stories, form their own interpretations and discuss them together.
[05:11] HELEN: I didn't realise that. So interpretation won't appear in the report?

[05:17] JEREMY: No. We do need a section on the illustrations because pictures are central to a child's experience of a story. Since you understand drawing better, it might be easiest for you to write it.
[05:32] HELEN: Perhaps, but I find that topic difficult to explain in writing. I'd prefer you to take that section.
[05:40] JEREMY: All right. When do you think?
[05:45] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Ethnography In Business
content: 📌 Ethnography in Business
Ethnography: research into human cultures
Business applications
examining customers’ needs and [ _____ ]supporting the development of new designs

Examples of ethnographic research in business
Kitchen equipment:
Researchers discovered that cooks had difficulty seeing the [ _____ ] inside measuring cups.
Cell phones:
In Uganda, people paid entrepreneurs to use their mobile phones.Customers wished to monitor the [ _____ ] they had used.
Computer companies:
New [ _____ ] was required to help system administrators exchange information with colleagues.
Hospitals:
Nurses needed information about [ _____ ] wherever they were in the hospital.
Airlines:
During journeys, respondents recorded their [ _____ ].
Principles of ethnographic research in business

Selection criteria may include age, [ _____ ] or the product used.Participants need to feel [ _____ ] about joining the research.Participants are generally studied through direct [ _____ ].The participant determines the direction of the interview.Considerable time is required for data [ _____ ].Researchers seek a meaningful pattern across the data.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about the use of ethnography in business. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today, I'm going to discuss ethnography, a form of research that examines how human cultures function.

[00:55] AUDIO: It originated in anthropology and has also been applied in sociology and communication studies. You may wonder how this relates to business. Companies have discovered that ethnography provides a deeper understanding of what current and future customers may need, while also revealing their attitudes towards products that already exist. It can further assist businesses in designing products or services that customers genuinely want.

[01:29] AUDIO: Consider some commercial examples. A research team once worked for a manufacturer of kitchen equipment. By watching cooks use measuring cups for ingredients such as flour and sugar, the researchers noticed repeated checking. Although numbers were printed inside the cups, users found them difficult to see.

[01:50] AUDIO: The company therefore developed a redesigned cup that solved the problem, and it became a best seller. Another ethnographic study examined mobile phone use in Uganda. People without phones of their own paid local entrepreneurs to make calls on their devices. Because the calls were paid for in advance, customers wanted to know how much time they had already used.

[02:18] AUDIO: In response, the manufacturer added this function to phones intended for international markets. Ethnographic methods have also been employed by computer companies. At one organization, researchers observed IT system administrators for several weeks. Much of their work required communication with colleagues to resolve problems, yet they had no standard method for sharing information from spreadsheets and similar sources.

[02:50] AUDIO: The research team proposed software that would make this exchange easier. A separate team observed and interviewed hospital nurses. It became clear that nurses needed access to information about their patients wherever they happened to be in the hospital. This finding led to a portable tablet that allowed them to consult records throughout the building.

[03:17] AUDIO: Sometimes the researchers cannot enter the environment being studied. During one airline project, for instance, passengers used smartphones to record information throughout their journeys. The study tracked their emotions during the flight. How do these studies differ from conventional research?

[03:42] AUDIO: Let's consider the main principles of commercial ethnography. First, the researcher begins without a hypothesis to test and must remain entirely open-minded, allowing the participants to provide the direction. Selecting those participants is fairly similar to ordinary research. Criteria may include a particular age group, a certain income level or use of a specific product.

[04:12] AUDIO: Recruiting suitable people is essential. Beyond meeting the chosen criteria, participants must feel comfortable discussing themselves and being observed during their normal activities. Researchers often find that people become open quite readily, perhaps because the study commonly occurs in their home or workplace. A defining feature is that the method does not simply rely on questionnaires.

[04:42] AUDIO: It usually involves direct first-hand observation of participants while they act. Researchers may still talk with them, but unlike a traditional interview, the participant determines the direction of the conversation. This reduces the chance that the researcher's assumptions will shape the responses. The work continues long after the researchers leave the participants.

[05:08] AUDIO: Many estimate that 70-80% of their time goes not into gathering material, but into its analysis. Examining photographs, listening to recordings and producing transcripts. They may accumulate hundreds of pages of notes. To decide what matters, they avoid concentrating only on dramatic or unusual details.

[05:35] AUDIO: Instead, they search across the data for a meaningful pattern and interpret what lies behind it. The resulting insights can influence the entire design process. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking at a box office about activities during the Stretton Festival. First, you have some time to look at questions one to seven. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to seven.
[00:48] ROB: Good morning. Stretton Festival box office, how may I help?

[00:54] MELANIE: Hello, my family and I are holidaying in the area and we've noticed posters for this week's festival. Could you give me some information about the events? To begin with, can we still get tickets for Saturday's jazz band?
[01:09] ROB: Yes, although only the 18 pounds tickets remain. All the 12 pound seats have sold out.
[01:16] MELANIE: Fine. The performance is at the school, isn't it?

[01:20] ROB: That's right, the secondary school. Be careful not to go to the primary school. There will also be a guest musician who isn't named on the posters. Carolyn Hart is performing with the band.
[01:32] MELANIE: I think I've heard her on the radio. Does she play the oboe? Or perhaps the flute?
[01:39] ROB: The flute. She normally performs with symphony orchestras and this appears to be her first concert with a jazz band.
[01:48] MELANIE: I'd certainly like to hear that. I also wanted to ask about the duck races. I saw a poster by the river. How do they work?

[01:58] ROB: You purchase one or more yellow plastic ducks for one pound each and write your name on them. The number of entries will determine how many races are held. A local champion swimmer, John Stevens, will launch them. The ducks enter the river behind the cinema and travel 500 meters to the railway bridge.
[02:20] MELANIE: Are prizes awarded?
[02:22] ROB: Yes. The owner of the first duck across the finish in each race receives free tickets for the concert held on the festival's final evening.
[02:33] MELANIE: Where can we buy the ducks? Both my children will want one.
[02:37] ROB: A stall in the market sells them. It's easy to spot because of the enormous sign featuring two ducks.
[02:45] MELANIE: I'll visit it this afternoon. I passed the market yesterday. Could you also tell me about the flower show?
[02:53] ROB: Admission is free and it takes place in Bythwaite Hall.
[02:56] MELANIE: Could you spell that?
[02:59] ROB: B-Y-T-H-W-A-I-T-E. Bythwaite.
[03:07] MELANIE: Is the hall easy to locate? I don't know the town well yet.
[03:12] ROB: You'll have no difficulty. It's in Central Stretton and is the town's only old building, so it stands out.
[03:19] MELANIE: I know the place. Is the show open throughout the day?
[03:24] ROB: Yes, but to watch the prizes for the best flowers being presented arrive by five. A well-known actor, Kevin Chapless, will present them. He lives nearby and supports many local events.
[03:38] MELANIE: I've seen him on television. I'll definitely attend the presentation.
[03:43] ROB: Good.
[03:47] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions eight to ten. Now listen and answer questions eight to ten.
[04:31] MELANIE: I found a list of plays being staged this week. I'd like to know which ones suit my children and which my husband and I might attend.
[04:39] ROB: How old are your children?
[04:42] MELANIE: Five and seven. What can you tell me about the mystery of Muldoon?
[04:46] ROB: It's designed for children aged five to ten.
[04:50] MELANIE: So my children would probably enjoy it more than I would?

[04:53] ROB: Yes. If you want a production for you and your husband while a babysitter watches the children, consider Fire and Flood. It recounts events that occurred in Stretton two centuries ago, and younger viewers may find it frightening.
[05:09] MELANIE: Thank you for warning me. Finally, what about Silly Sailor?
[05:14] ROB: It's a comedy intended for both younger and older audiences. In fact, it received an award at the Stretton Drama Festival two months ago.
[05:23] MELANIE: Great. Goodbye. And thank you for all the details. I'm really looking forward to the festival.
[05:31] ROB: Goodbye.
[05:35] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Newly Reopened Museum
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Newly Reopened Museum"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a museum guide describing several collections. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Good morning, and welcome to our museum, which contains an extraordinary range of exhibits.

[00:54] AUDIO: I'm Greg, and I'll describe the collections as we tour the building. Before we set off, though, let me give you an idea of what you can see. First, the museum owns an excellent group of 20th and 21st century paintings, including works by many famous artists. You will probably recognize a number of them.

[01:19] AUDIO: This gallery contains the museum's most popular exhibits and attracts more visitors than any other, so come early before it becomes crowded. We also display 19th century paintings. When the museum opened in the middle of that century, several individual artists donated one work each to help establish the collection. Those personal gifts give the paintings particular significance for us.

[01:47] AUDIO: The sculpture gallery contains several outstanding pieces, but it is temporarily closed for renovation. You'll need to return next year to see the whole collection together. For now, some sculptures have been transferred to other areas of the museum. Around the World is a temporary exhibition that has recently received coverage on television and in newspapers.

[02:14] AUDIO: It has attracted considerable attention by presenting objects from every continent and many different nations, along with explanations of their social context. Why each object was produced and who used it. Next is our specialist coin collection. Every coin comes from this country and dates from between one and two thousand years ago.

[02:39] AUDIO: Many were found by members of the public while digging in their gardens and were subsequently donated to the museum. Finally, the entire porcelain and glass collection was left by the museum's founder when he died in 1878. His will prevents us from adding any further items because he considered the collection complete and we agree with him. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
[03:44] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. That gives you an overview of the collections. I'll now provide some practical information. Most visitor facilities are in the basement.

[04:01] AUDIO: At the foot of these stairs you enter a sitting area furnished with chairs and sofas where you can rest during your visit. Our restaurant offers high quality meals throughout the day in a calm setting. From the bottom of the stairs walk straight across to the far side of the sitting area and turn right into the corridor. The restaurant entrance will be directly in front of you.

[04:27] AUDIO: For a snack or somewhere better equipped for children there is also a cafe. Again, walk across the sitting area and turn right into the corridor. The cafe is the first door immediately on your right. The basement also contains baby changing facilities.

[04:44] AUDIO: Cross the sitting area and continue into the corridor on the left. The facilities are located on the left hand side. Please leave coats, umbrellas, and large bags in the cloak room. It is on the left of the sitting area through the final door before the corridor.

[05:03] AUDIO: Toilets are available on every floor. In the basement they are the first rooms on your left after you come down the stairs. If you need to use the cloak room please do so now and then we'll begin the tour. That is the end of part two.
[05:22] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Research On Female Musical Performers
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Research On Female Musical Performers"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a student discussing her previous psychology research with her supervisor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.

[00:51] SUPERVISOR: Hello, Joanna. It's good to see you. Before we consider your new project, I'd like to hear about the psychology study you completed for your masters last year. So how did you select the participants?

[01:06] JOANNA: I worked with six professional female musicians. They included violinists, a cellist, a pianist and a flautist. All were highly respected and each had toured extensively across several continents. A number had also received prizes in competitions.
[01:26] SUPERVISOR: They were fairly young, weren't they?

[01:29] JOANNA: Yeah, they ranged from 25 to 29 years old. Let's see. The mean was 27.8. I didn't deliberately recruit performers who had released recordings, but that is almost expected nowadays and every participant had done so.
[01:48] SUPERVISOR: You gathered the information through telephone interviews, correct?

[01:52] JOANNA: Yes. Because I wanted leading musicians who had very busy schedules, interviewing them by telephone was the only practical option. I used an adapter to record each call. I'd been concerned about sound quality, but there were no technical difficulties.
[02:14] JOANNA: Every interview lasted at least 30 minutes and some were longer.
[02:19] SUPERVISOR: Did the telephone create a stressful atmosphere?

[02:24] JOANNA: I expected that possibility, but the discussions were informal and the musicians were eager to speak. The method certainly didn't reduce the richness of the data. If anything, it produced more detailed responses.
[02:41] SUPERVISOR: Your subject was performers' clothing at concerts?

[02:45] JOANNA: Yes. The eventual study examined how musicians understood their professional role and how that influenced what they wore. But that focus developed gradually. Initially, I intended to investigate how audiences reacted to performers' clothing and whether the instrument played, for example violin, flute or trumpet, was connected to the style selected.
[03:13] SUPERVISOR: It's notable that performers normally decide for themselves what to wear.
[03:19] JOANNA: Yes. You might expect orchestras to impose formal rules, but they rarely do.
[03:28] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:11] SUPERVISOR: Your participants were all women. Was that because men care less about fashion?

[04:18] JOANNA: Many male musicians follow fashion closely. Socially, however, they have a much narrower range of acceptable clothing and audiences would react badly if they moved beyond those limits.
[04:33] SUPERVISOR: Popular music follows different conventions. Have you read Mike Frost's article on female performers' clothes in popular music?
[04:42] JOANNA: No, I haven't.

[04:43] SUPERVISOR: He observes that many female singers and instrumentalists dress informally and choose less traditionally feminine items, such as jeans rather than skirts. His explanation is that otherwise people may dismiss them as trivial rather than take their work seriously.
[05:03] JOANNA: Practicality might also explain it. Popular music concerts are often extremely energetic.
[05:10] SUPERVISOR: He doesn't discuss that, although I think you may be right. I was interested in the audience's influence on clothing choices.

[05:20] JOANNA: The musicians I interviewed considered the audience very important. They viewed a performance as a public occasion with certain expectations. Meeting those expectations through their choice of clothing was a way of showing respect for the audience.
[05:38] SUPERVISOR: So they didn't mind appearing to have made an effort.
[05:42] JOANNA: Exactly. In the past, audience members probably had similar expectations of one another, but that is less true today, at least in the UK.
[05:53] SUPERVISOR: I agree.
[05:55] JOANNA: I also became interested in sports scientists' research on clothing.

[06:00] SUPERVISOR: Musicians face physical risks because their movements are intensive and highly repetitive. Some features used in sportswear might therefore protect performers from injuries caused by those movements.
[06:15] JOANNA: Yes, but musicians seldom consider that. They avoid obviously restrictive clothes, but generally go no further.
[06:23] SUPERVISOR: Returning to your own research, have you decided what to do next?
[06:27] JOANNA: I was considering a study involving an audience, including...
[06:36] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 The use of soil to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Rattan Lal

Soil and carbon

Regenerative agriculture

California study

Australian study

Possible future developments

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about using soil to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. As we learned in the previous lecture, the rapid increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide over the past century is a major driver of climate change.

[00:59] AUDIO: Reducing the quantity of carbon dioxide could therefore slow the rate of change. One possible approach is to improve the ability of the soil supporting plants to absorb carbon dioxide. Ratan Lal, a soil scientist at Ohio State University in the United States, argues that agricultural soils worldwide could potentially take up 13% of the carbon dioxide currently in the atmosphere. That is equivalent to the amount emitted during the past 30 years.

[01:36] AUDIO: Researchers are now examining how to achieve this. Lal's original interest in soil did not arise from climate research. He was concerned about the land and the communities that relied upon it. Soil rich in carbon is dark, loose and productive, and it retains water.

[01:56] AUDIO: By contrast, erosion becomes more likely when soil is dry, often because it contains too little carbon. Such erosion makes both crop cultivation and livestock farming more difficult. During the 1970s and 1980s, Lal studied African soils with so little organic matter that the ground had become extremely hard, almost like concrete. There, he met an early researcher in global warming who proposed that the missing soil carbon had entered the atmosphere.

[02:32] AUDIO: Evidence increasingly supports that explanation. For millions of years, atmospheric carbon dioxide has been partly controlled through a natural partnership between plants and tiny organisms in the soil. Plants take carbon dioxide from the air and convert it into sugars and other carbon-containing materials. Some remain within the plant, while another portion pass up from the roots to fungi and soil microbes, which retain the carbon underground.

[03:09] AUDIO: The development of agriculture roughly 10,000 years ago disrupted these ancient processes and caused soil carbon loss. By draining and ploughing natural topsoil, people exposed buried carbon to oxygen. This produced carbon dioxide, which escaped into the atmosphere. In some places, grazing animals removed all the vegetation and released still more carbon.

[03:38] AUDIO: Huge quantities have been taken from the soil, where they are valuable and transferred to the air. What can be done? Research now indicates that even fairly small changes in farming practices may substantially reduce atmospheric carbon. Some farmers already follow regenerative agriculture.

[04:03] AUDIO: This uses established methods to increase fertility and keep soil moist. Examples include maintaining crops throughout the year and growing a greater variety of plants. These strategies can raise the amount of carbon stored underground, and agricultural researchers are building evidence for their use against climate change. One American project investigating carbon storage on agricultural land is underway in California.

[04:39] AUDIO: Wendy Silver, a soil scientist from the University of California, Berkeley, is leading a pioneering study on a large cattle farm. Her team is testing how carbon storage changes when compost is applied. The compost combines agricultural waste, including manure and maize stalks, with garden waste such as leaves, branches and grass cuttings. In Australia, soil ecologist Christine Jones is evaluating another promising method.

[05:14] AUDIO: Working with 12 farmers, she aims to raise the carbon content of soil by cultivating grasses that stay green throughout the year. Like compost application, the technique has already succeeded in experimental conditions. Jones now wants to prove it works on commercial farms, and that the captured carbon can be measured accurately. It is hoped that such projects will reveal how farmers and other land managers can help limit the harmful effects of greenhouse gases.

[05:51] AUDIO: In nations such as the United States, where farms commonly apply large quantities of fertilizer, changing established practice will require a new system. Lal believes farmers should receive payment not only for the crops or meat they sell, but also for the carbon retained in their soil. Another study currently being conducted. That is the end of Part 4.
[06:23] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4.
